utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Could the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. This is case number IT-05-88/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are still listening to you, Mr. Prosecutor. You have the floor, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to you and Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Mr. President, we left off with the devastating effects of Directive 7's policy to make life unbearable for the Muslim populations in Srebrenica and Zepa. The evidence will show that while the VRS slowly strangled the enclaves, strangled out life and hope of survival out of them, the VRS never took its eyes off of an opportunity to mount its own direct military attack on Srebrenica in order to fulfil Strategic Objectives 1 and 3. What we have here is a Main Staff order from May of 1995, and we can see what its objective is from the title: "Stabilise Defence and Create Conditions for Their Liberation." And if we look at the first paragraph, again there's a reference to according to the information gathered, that means intelligence, and in particular that means General Tolimir's intelligence, the Muslims are making intensive operations for an operation from the area of Tuzla, Kladanj, and the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa with the basic aim of cutting the territory of Republika Srpska, connecting the enclaves with the central part of the so-called Bosnia and Herzegovina, and reaching the Drina River. Again, which would impede the Serbs' Strategic Objectives of not having the Drina River as a boundary to their unified Serbian state. You're going to see during the trial follow-on orders from the Drina Corps based on this Main Staff order to do precisely that, mobilise the forces, get ready for combat pursuant to this order to liberate those enclaves in May. And then you'll see also additional orders back from the Drina Corps up to the Main Staff saying, "We cannot implement your order because we don't have enough forces to do so." But you will also see that the Drina Corps, always relentless in pursuit of Strategic Objective's 1 and 3, continued to modify its combat plan throughout the end of May with input from the Main Staff, so they would be in a position when the time came to take that decisive step. And during this period of time also, as always, we have General Tolimir on top of the intelligence picture, trying to get into the head of the enemy, trying to understand what the morale, intentions, plans of the enemy was and he issues his reports thought the month, noting, for example, in May a few days after this Main Staff order that the Muslim forces from the enclaves in the Podrinje have continued reconnaissance and diversionary operations, aimed at creating conditions for offensive operations which they intend to start by infiltrating forces into the rear and the disposition of our units. Other significant preparations for this decisive attack on the Srebrenica enclave were taken at the end of May. You may recall me mentioning a few times this observation post echo, one of the UN OPs, the south-east corner of the enclave which was lying on a militarily significant east-west road in the area of Zeleni Jadar. General Tolimir paid particular attention to that early in the year, as we talked about on Friday. And you will see at the end of May specific Drina Corps orders going out, to take that UN OP out, to take it out with force if necessary. And indeed, that's what happened. The Serbs attacked the UN observation post with machine-gun fire, tank, and rocket fire. Damaged the watch-tower in the process and forced those peacekeepers right out of that OP. And you'll see a videotape of a speech that the Drina Corps commander, General Zivanovic, gave on the 12th of July, celebrating the fall of Srebrenica and confirming that the attack on this OP had been the start, the prelude, to the VRS's ultimate take-over of the Srebrenica enclave. Very simply he said, and I quote: "At the beginning of June, more precisely at the end of May, we started to carry out preparations and then took Zeleni Jadar and tested what the expulsion of UNPROFOR with weapons looked like. Quite a lot of soldiers were involved and as it turned out that we had no casualties and no wounded, then slowly conditions ripened for what we did now." And you'll see that the importance of this military action was not lost on UNPROFOR, both because it signalled that the VRS was willing to use force, as they had seen before, against peacekeepers and also that it signalled a potential future attack on the enclave as a whole. And of course this attack disproves the lies you will hear General Tolimir, General Gvero, and General Mladic tell UNPROFOR in the midst of the VRS attack in July that we would never attack UNPROFOR, we hope UNPROFOR would never be our enemy. We're not attacking anyone. The evidence will be clear that when the UN got in the way of the VRS, the VRS was willing to take peacekeepers hostage, to threaten their lives, to threaten to kill them, to fire at observation posts at DutchBat positions with machine-guns, rockets, and tanks while peacekeepers were in them. And as always you'll see that they knew just how far to go, knowing the risk that if they stepped over the line and went too far, the UN might invoke its ability to use air power, again, the one weapon that the UN had at that time in the area because the peacekeepers on the ground in Srebrenica had been so operationally undermined by Directive 7's restrictions at that time. There was nothing else that they could do but rely on close air support or air-strikes. And you'll see as we near the end of June more reports from General Tolimir never taking his eyes off the enclaves. You'll see his intelligence reports focusing on their intentions, the impending combat activities. And you'll see him reporting before and after the Muslims, at the end of June, conducted some raids, sabotage raids, which resulted in the deaths of Serb soldiers and civilians. And you may hear reference to these raids, in particular on a village called Vizjnica where civilians were killed by the Muslim saboteurs. But as the evidence will show, Your Honours, these hit-and-run attacks by these Muslim sabotage squads would serve really just as a pretext for taking the final steps towards fulfilling Strategic Objectives 1 and 3 which had always been there from day one. So we see by July that the VRS has made its decision to attack Srebrenica. What have you on your screen is General Zivanovic's Drina Corps order to attack the enclave. The code-name for the operation Krivaja 95, order for active combat operations number 1, 2 July. And you'll see that this order, like an earlier one that he issued that day, a preparatory or warning order as they're called, explicitly refers to Directives 7 and it's follow-on 7/1. The Drina Corps command pursuant to those operations directives and on the basis of the situation in the corps has the task of carrying out offensive activities with free forces deep in the Drina Corps zone as soon as possible in order to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica. Now, with respect to this objective of splitting the enclaves apart, we've heard that before. Sealing off the enclaves from each other so there could be no passage of men, materiel, make it more difficult for them to defend themselves in isolation from each other. And this was a legitimate military objective, to ensure that demilitarisation of the enclave. But we see that General Zivanovic again takes the extra step and orders that the army reduce the enclaves to their urban areas. Now, this necessarily meant forcing the civilian population into the very concentrated centre areas of Srebrenica and Zepa. The VRS and General Tolimir well knew that this would create conditions whereby it would be impossible for the Muslim population of those enclaves to sustain themselves. They knew that this would replicate the humanitarian disaster of 1993, and they knew based on what they saw in 1993 -- you remember the video, people clamouring on to those UNHCR buses to get trucked out in empty lorries, out of that misery. People crushed to death, suffocated to death in the press to escape the hell of Srebrenica in 1993. General Tolimir and the VRS knew in 1995 that not only would they be replicating those conditions, the conditions would be worse because in July of 1995 Directive 7 had been implemented with ruthless efficiency for months. And make no mistake about it, Your Honours, some military policeman manning a check-point, stripping a convoy of humanitarian aid might not know any better. But the highest-level officers in the VRS like General Tolimir, they knew better. You saw those SFRY regulations, you saw the VRS laws and rules that incorporated the Geneva Conventions and crimes against humanity. They knew that targeting civilians was wrong. They knew that that convoy terror was a crime. He knew that every denied convoy brought the civilian population further to its knees, just like 1993. But he chose to keep moving that plan along. So by its very words in July of 1995, the Krivaja 95 combat plan, given the conditions that prevailed in Srebrenica in July of 1995, it must be understood as implementing Directive 7's direction, to make life unbearable for the Muslim populations of Zepa and Srebrenica with no hope for survival. The departure of the civilian populations from those enclaves was therefore not a collateral consequence of that combat order. The decision to reduce it to the urban enclaves and the departure of the Muslim population from them was a clear and clearly illegal objective of this combat operation. And we'll see in August of 1995, Your Honours, President Karadzic himself again acknowledging that this was about the strategic importance of Srebrenica and Zepa, addressing the 53rd National Assembly on 28 August of 1995, and I quote: "We absolutely cannot let ourselves get any ideas about them taking our traditional territories from us. To tell the truth, there are towns that we have grabbed for ourselves and there are only 30 per cent of us. I can name as many of those as you want, but we cannot give up the towns where we made up 70 per cent. Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us there were in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica, in Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance, they had to become ours. And no one is practically questioning it anymore." Black and white, acknowledging that these were predominantly Muslim enclaves and for strategic reasons they had to become Serb. That's what it was really about. That's what Krivaja 95 was really about, and a copy of that was sent to the Main Staff. The Main Staff continued to follow that operation. And more importantly for our purposes you will see how the Main Staff with significant contributions from General Tolimir neutralised UNPROFOR during this attack and facilitated the VRS's take-over of the enclave. So let me turn now to the attack itself. It began on the 6th of July. VRS tanks, artillery, aerial bombs, mortars, rockets, heavy machine-guns pounded the entire enclave. You'll hear that the DutchBat deputy commander, Major Franken, stated that the shelling in Srebrenica was random and that DutchBat was already transporting wounded civilians to the Srebrenica hospital. What we have here is an excerpt from a United Nations Military Observer report. They were known as UNMOs, the abbreviation. This is a report from somebody you'll hear from and see a lot of, actually, in the video footage, an officer named Joseph Kingori, who was in Srebrenica when the shells began raining down. And we see here he reports a BSA offensive, again, BSA meaning VRS. He identifies all manner of weapons, artillery, falling on Potocari township, Srebrenica township, at least 250 artillery and mortar rounds have been recorded so far. Fatalities confirmed, DutchBat compound rockets landing. And you'll see OP Foxtrot coming under direct shelling by the VRS. Colonel Kingori reported that several tank rounds were fired directly at OP Foxtrot, destroying the watch-tower. And he later reported that an artillery impact killed a civilian and injured a boy. He said that when he was in Srebrenica he would notice that the shells would fall about 50 at a time and then slowly sweep across the town and then back in the other direction after a pause in between. You'll hear that the shelling was indiscriminate, hitting civilian targets, causing injuries. And you'll hear again that DutchBat OPs and positions were targeted with all manner of weaponry. The entrance to the Potocari compound constantly the target of suppressing fire, close fire, not right at the compound, inside the compound, but right in front of it, suppressing fire. It was obvious to the peacekeepers that it was meant to keep DutchBat inside its compound during the early portions of the attack. You'll hear that when the peacekeepers a couple of days into the attack were ordered to form blocking positions, that is, drive their APCs to a particular location in the south of the enclave as a sort of line in the sand, across which if the VRS passed it would invoke close air support, you'll see that when those peacekeepers were sitting in their APCs in their blocking positions, they were shelled. What we have on our screen is an interim combat report. You've already heard me talk about the importance of the reporting, how that was a regular part of the professionalism of this army, and here we have from the forward command post you'll see Pribicevac, that's a location to the east of the Srebrenica enclave where General Krstic basically had his command post for the purposes of this operation setup. And it also afforded a lookout of the enclave. So that's where he's sending this from. And you'll see right in the beginning: "Pursuant to the order of the GS VRS," again that's Main Staff, Glavni Stab, "and the decision of the Drina Corps commander to separate and reduce the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, combat activities around the Srebrenica enclave proceeded." He makes a decision for continuing the operations: "Continue the attack energetically and extremely decisively with the objective of completing sealing off and reducing the Srebrenica enclave to the inner town area." And again we're talking about basically a small network of streets and buildings, and he's again referring to the inner town area, reducing that population that had been had been living in and around Srebrenica to that compressed location. And you'll see in -- during the trial General Krstic actually does issue an attack order that night. Meanwhile, as we see from this report from the UNMOs on the 7th DutchBat is reporting heavy shelling around the Potocari compound, more injuries, more shells landing in Srebrenica. Kingori will tell you that one of them died at the Srebrenica hospital. He was personally involved. You will hear from Colonel Kingori that he was out and about, and you'll see him out and about, somebody trying to do something about the horror he found himself in the middle of. The next excerpt from this report is dated at 1400 hours. Please note the UNMOs are observing that the VRS offensive seems to be steadily intensifying. Whatever their aims are, they seem to be concentrating more on civilian targets in Srebrenica town and Potocari. There are civilian casualties and unassessed damage to civilian property." When Colonel Kingori and his fellow UNMO had the time to count, they counted over 200 shells hitting Srebrenica that day. By the next morning the shelling was continuing. We see here from this report it started at 0800, and I quote: "They seem to be concentrating more on the densely populated areas ... and Potocari town ..." again targeting the civilians. You'll hear that on this day, the 8th of July, the Serbs captured three observation posts in the southern part of the enclave, foxtrot, uniform, and sierra, all in the general area of OP Echo that you heard about before. So you have forces moving south up towards Srebrenica town from the south of the enclave. And you'll hear that at OP Foxtrot, a Serb tank was firing directly at the OP, causing the peacekeepers to withdraw in their APC under that tank fire. And you'll hear that when they did so there were some Muslim fighters nearby. And you'll hear that these Muslim fighters for a period of time put up some resistance to the VRS attack, were positioning themselves in between the UN OPs. So you'll hear that when this UN APC was trying to withdraw because the Serb tank was trying to blast it out of its OP, you'll hear that the Muslims didn't want these UN peacekeepers to leave, fearing that this would speed the collapse of the enclave. So one of them fired at the APC and ended up killing a DutchBat soldier. Now, it is in the afternoon of the 8th of July that General Tolimir and UNPROFOR Generals Nicolai and Janvier begin having a series of telephone conversations about the attack. General Nicolai was a Dutch general who was based in the Sarajevo UNPROFOR command. He was General Smith's Chief of Staff. General Smith was commander of the UN forces in Bosnia. And during the attack, you'll hear that General Smith was actually on leave, out of theatre, so General Nicolai ended up having a lot of contact with the Main Staff. And you'll also hear that another UNPROFOR general, General Gobillard, a French general, who was head of the Sarajevo sector of UNPROFOR also had contact with the Main Staff. General Gobillard, of course, also served underneath Smith, but he was head of a separate office, if you will, that was based in Sarajevo. And you'll also hear conversations involving General Janvier, as I mentioned. General Janvier was another French general who was head of all the UN forces in that theatre. He was based in Zagreb. And he was General Smith's direct superior. So you have Janvier, Smith, Nicolai, Gobillard. Now, again and again you'll hear, Your Honours, the conversations between General Tolimir and these UN generals would go something like this: UNPROFOR would tell General Tolimir: Your forces are attacking. They're attacking UNPROFOR positions. They're attacking civilian targets, as was abundantly clear from the reports flooding in from all sources to UNPROFOR. Tolimir would then deny to whichever general he was speaking, that the VRS was attacking anyone. He would make the counter allegation that the Muslims were the ones attacking and violating the prior agreements. He would claim that his information conflicted with UNPROFOR's. He needed time to contact his subordinate commanders or his superior or to issue orders, consult with Mladic, that he needed more time to verify the information on the ground, but the information he was getting was wrong. In any case, you'll hear him repeatedly postponing further contact with the UN. And as you will hear, Your Honours, this was a deliberate delaying tactic that permitted General Krstic's forces to encroach further and further into the enclave, advancing towards the ultimate target of eliminating the enclave. Even as General Tolimir was insisting that they were not attacking. And you just saw that 6 July interim combat report where General Krstic is talking about taking a decisive attack, pressing forward. So what you see here is a Drina Corps report. It's signed by General Zivanovic on the 8th of July, and this is going out to the Drina Corps IKM, to General Krstic, because General Zivanovic is now back in Vlasenica at the Drina Corps command. And what he says is, as we can see from the slide, the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo has protested with the Main Staff over operations against UNPROFOR observation point, and he gives some co-ordinates. And that's the -- that's OP Foxtrot, the one that you'll hear got blasted by the VRS tank resulting in the death of that soldier by the Muslims. But that's what he's talking about there, this direct fire by the Serb tank on this OP. And again, the complaint is specific. They emphasise that their point was captured by artillery and tank action and the Main Staff of the VRS answered that the Drina Corps command had informed it that the Muslims were using six armoured personnel carriers painted white and bearing UNPROFOR markings and that the Muslims had started offensive operations from Srebrenica in order to join up the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. So General Zivanovic is here reporting what the Main Staff is trying to sell to UNPROFOR in Sarajevo when they complain. And again, there may have been some hit-and-run sabotage missions by the Muslims at the end of June, which may have been the last straw, but as we have seen and as the evidence will show, this mission, this combat operation against Srebrenica, had been in the works for a long time and the moment had come. And again, the Main Staff, according to Zivanovic's report, accusing the Muslims of not demilitarising, which they hadn't, and demanding UNPROFOR to get their observation posts in the right places. And then finally: "The Main Staff has ordered you not to attack UNPROFOR, but to prevent any surprises and stop the Muslims in their intention to join up Srebrenica and Zepa." Now, again this is reflective not on -- not of some kind of humanitarian motives, but it's the Main Staff, General Tolimir in particular because you'll see from the greeting here at the end: "Good luck in war and best regards from General Tolimir." General Tolimir is either at the Drina Corps command with General Zivanovic at this time or he's communicating with General Zivanovic from the Main Staff. But either way, when we're talking about the Main Staff here, we're talking about General Tolimir, as we've already seen from the conversations. And this is General Tolimir again understanding that there's only so far they can go before UNPROFOR will call in air support or air-strikes. They know just how far they can go. And you'll see that in their response to UNPROFOR, it's very careful. They can't deny that their tanks are attacking, because the Muslims certainly didn't have tanks, so they make counter allegations and deflect what the real issue is. We just have here one of a series of protest notes that you'll see more examples of. General Nicolai putting in -- into their files at the UN the note that he talked to General Tolimir this afternoon about the VRS attack on OP Foxtrot. Although General Tolimir promised that UNPROFOR and UN positions would not be attacked, now two UNPROFOR positions about 500 metres west of the OP Foxtrot have been surrounded by your troops, VRS troops. Those are the two OPs, sierra and uniform, which were in fact set up when the VRS blew OP Echo out that we talked about before. And you'll hear that those OPs were surrounded and the peacekeepers surrendered. At this time we see the Main Staff becoming even more involved. This is a request from the same day on the 8th from General Zivanovic, asking the Main Staff to crank up its propaganda activities towards the enclave. We saw some examples on Friday of, again, Zivanovic reaching out to General Gvero to try and encourage the Muslim population to leave, how to manage that in the midst of the horror that they'd created. And what we'll see here is that very soon Lieutenant-Colonel Milovan Milutinovic, who was the chief of the Main Staff's press centre, is dispatched to Srebrenica and he's on the ground. You'll see him present at the Hotel Fontana meetings and later at Zepa, and those were all filmed. They were filmed purely for propaganda purposes and they were used to great effect by the VRS. And you'll see General Tolimir ordering loudspeakers for Colonel Milutinovic in Zepa when we get to that section. So we have the Main Staff further and further involved. General Nicolai, we're into the next day, the 9th, in the afternoon. The attack just keeps pressing forward. Nothing is stopping the VRS. One by one you'll hear they would surround, fire at the observation posts, and that the peacekeepers would surrender. In some cases they would surrender under fire and by threat of force by the VRS, and you'll hear that in other cases they surrendered more or less voluntarily because they were afraid of being caught in cross-fire between what few Muslim fighters remained and the VRS tank, machine-gun mortar, and rocket fire. And you'll hear that some of them were afraid of being targeted by the Muslims, again as that one soldier had been the day before. So we have General Nicolai getting more and more concerned. The troops have penetrated 4 kilometres into the safe area and are a kilometre away from the centre of town. He's insisting that they -- that the VRS withdraw, and General Tolimir's response was that his information about the situation was different. Nicolai warned that DutchBat would now have to defend the safe area, and again repeated his request to withdraw. General Tolimir's response, he promised he would check the information directly on the ground, although he did not believe this was true and asked General Nicolai to call back in 30 minutes. A little while later -- the Court's indulgence. You'll hear that General Janvier from Zagreb gets involved. Remember, Nicolai is in Sarajevo. Janvier calls the Main Staff and leaves a message. You'll see this, and I quote, very simple message: "You are to withdraw your soldiers who are on the offensive around Srebrenica by 8.00 tomorrow morning." So we have another conversation with General Nicolai and General Tolimir after that warning is given by the force commander himself, General Janvier. Tolimir assures Nicolai that he had passed on the message to his subordinate commanders and that the VRS had no particular problems with UNPROFOR or the civil population in Srebrenica and that the UNPROFOR soldiers were treated correctly. Nicolai is not having it. He's insisting on their withdrawal. He says there's going to be a strong warning issued supported by General Janvier and Mr. Akashi, the special representative of the UN Secretary-General. General Tolimir confirms that he understands the message and repeated that there was no conflict between UNPROFOR, the VRS, and the civilian population in Srebrenica. Again, turning it around, the only problems they had were those ones relevant to the BiH army, the Muslim army, and the southern section of the Srebrenica enclave and to the BiH attempt to link the enclave of Zepa and that of Srebrenica. The BiH offensive taken from inside the demilitarised zone had been prevented by the VRS. It is the BiH offensive actions taken from the demilitarised zone that constituted the violation. Nicolai repeats that what Tolimir said has absolutely nothing to do with anything. He says their attack is threatening the civilian population of Srebrenica and was a direct attack on the safe area. And again, General Tolimir just keeps it up. He says that the Muslims were using heavy weapons, APCs. General Nicolai vehemently denies any DutchBat APCs were being used, that it was false information. Nicolai warns that the UN was going to have to use whatever means it had to defend the enclave. So this triggers the following document from General Tolimir later that evening. This goes out at 2025 or -- we see a time stamp that it was at least received at 2025 the night of the 9th. It's sent from the Drina Corps command in Vlasenica, the command post, which suggests because it has General Tolimir's type signature that General Tolimir was located at that time at the command. And that makes sense. Again, the Main Staff's preference for placing its generals forward so they can direct the action, influence what's happening on the ground. Here General Tolimir is reporting on what we just saw, General Nikolai's requests for withdrawal. And he's also reporting General Janvier's request to withdraw that we just saw a minute ago. And what does General Tolimir tell the commanders on the ground: "I replied to the UNPROFOR commander that I was checking the information about the situation in Srebrenica, and that their forces were safe. I anticipate talking to them in 40 minutes. "Send a battle-field situation report every hour so that I can communicate with UNPROFOR which will enable you to continue to work according to plan ..." And then again: "Pay particular attention to protecting members of UNPROFOR and the civilian population. "I congratulate you on your results and I wish you good fortunes of war." Which will enable you to continue to work according to plan, there it is. General Tolimir knows what the plan is. He's part of the plan and he's doing what he can to buy General Krstic and his troops more time so that they can finish the plan. He knows he can't put off the UN forever. He needs to tell them something. He needs to buy them time and he knows an hour is a long time, so that will give them some cover. But as he says, "it will enable you to continue to work according to plan." And again he knows just how far he can go. He says, "pay particular attention to protecting members of UNPROFOR." Blast them out of their OPs, if that's what it takes to get them out of the OPs, but don't go any further. Later that night, you recall General Nicolai said there's going to be a strong warning in writing, and here it is. It refers to the VRS attacks, firing indiscriminately into the safe area, directly targeting UN facilities causing several civilian deaths. These are the facts that are being reported from the ground to the UN. We have continued to fire heavy weapons into the safe area 1 kilometre from the south of the town. Another demand to stop and pull back. And here the UN is telling the VRS in no uncertain terms: We are setting up those blocking positions I mentioned a few moments ago with the APCs. The SRSG, that's the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, Mr. Akashi, and the FC, that's the force commander, General Janvier, have decided that if this blocking position is attacked, NATO close air support will be employed. A little later that night, about 2310 hours, we see an intercept. T here is for Tolimir. And I think we -- in this intercept we only get one side of the conversation. We only get what General Tolimir is saying. And he says: "I got the message from the General's courier," clearing referring to the warning that was issued. And this is, by the way, an intercept between General Tolimir and General Janvier. So it's gone to the top of the UN command. He's saying: I got the warning. And again, General Tolimir repeats the mantra: "Our army has very proper relations with the members of UNPROFOR as well as with the Muslim population. "Proper, very proper." And again he turns it around, the counter allegations. "The next thing is: The General is probably aware that the Muslims have been attacking in the last few days and they burned down some of our villages." Janvier has clearly repeated the UN insistence that the VRS pull back. General Tolimir says: "I understand the General ... I understand the General, but it is very difficult at this moment to make any movements since the entire area is an active front line ..." And he claims: "At this moment I can't even see the whole picture." You can tell from General Tolimir's next answer that Janvier is insisting that they pull back, and Tolimir says: "That's particularly difficult to do when the Muslims are attacking on nearly all fronts around the enclave. "I understand the General and I thank him, but it is difficult to talk about withdrawal before achieving combat activities." And he's assuring General Janvier that he'll talk to General Mladic, and he insists that: "We are doing our best to stabilise the situation as soon as possible ..." saying it's quite complicated, quite complicated. "I thank the General and also wish to give him a personal message, that we will do everything we can to calm down the situation and to find a reasonable solution." All right. Well, let's look at the situation and find out what General Tolimir really did to calm it down. Here's another interim combat report from General Krstic that night, and this is time stamped at 2320 hours. So pretty much at the same time that General Tolimir was just speaking to General Janvier, General Krstic issues this -- sends up this interim combat report from Pribicevac. And he starts off saying: "On the 9th of July ... our units carried out a fierce attack ... thus separating the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, carried out the immediate task and created conditions for extending the attack towards Srebrenica ..." and points out some of the features that they were able to capture. So General Krstic puts in his proposal, his decision what he wants to do: "Taking advantage of the success achieved, regroup the forces and carry out a vigorous and decisive attack towards Srebrenica." And again, this is at about 2320, according to one of the time stamps on this document. So what do we see General Tolimir doing next, having given his personal guarantee to calm down the situation? He sends this out. You'll see that this is coming from the Main Staff of the VRS, so this indicates that General Tolimir is back at the command post of the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka when he writes this. You'll notice also the series of numbers at the very top left of the screen. Strictly confidential number 12/46. You'll see when we get used to looking at more and more of these documents that these numbers mean something. That 12/46 designates General Tolimir's sector, and in particular 46 designates the security administration within the intelligence and security sector. So this is literally coming out of his shop. It's going out under his signature. And you'll note, if you please, also the time stamp showing that this is going out at 2350 hours, or at least that's one of the time-stamps that it was received. And you'll see that it's not difficult for General Tolimir to get back and forth from Crna Rijeka to Vlasenica. They're just down the road, Han Pijesak and Crna Rijeka are just down the road. Now, he sends it to President Karadzic and as we see here to Generals Gvero and General Krstic personally at that forward command post in Pribicevac. Obviously Tolimir and the -- his other Main Staff colleagues have been in contact and communications with each other because he knows General Gvero and there, he knows to address this personally to General Gvero. And why is General Gvero at Pribicevac? He's there to represent the Main Staff. Mladic is somewhere else in the field. Gvero is his man on the ground at Pribicevac to assess the situation, be informed by Krstic if there are any additional steps that need to be taken, what the problems are, to be able to provide guidance and to be able to relate that information in real time back to the Main Staff. This is how the VRS operated. General Tolimir passes on this critical information that President Karadzic has been informed of these successful combat operations around Srebrenica, that they have achieved results which enable them to occupy the very town of Srebrenica. So General Tolimir obviously is getting very, very timely information about what's going on on the ground, and he's relaying that to Karadzic: "The President of the Republic is satisfied with the results ... and has agreed with the continuation of operations for the take-over of Srebrenica, disarming the Muslim terrorist gangs and complete demilitarisation of the Srebrenica enclave." And you'll note here that Karadzic has agreed. What he's agreeing with is the proposal by the Main Staff to complete the operation, to complete the take-over. You saw General Krstic's interim combat report. That information gets communicated directly to General Tolimir. It's clear that Tolimir has been in personal contact with President Karadzic, personal communications, or he has been fully informed by somebody else, perhaps General Mladic, who has. Because General Mladic must have approved this decision as well. And again: "The President of Republika Srpska has ordered that in the follow-up combat operations, full protection to UNPROFOR ... Muslim civilian population ... guaranteed safety ..." You see specific instructions: "... maximum protection and safety ... refrain from destroying civilian targets ..." And again, this is not born of some humanitarian motive on the part of President Karadzic and the Main Staff. They know how close they are to completing the objectives of Strategic Objective 1 and 3. They know how close they are and they don't want to screw it up. They don't want the international community to be triggered, to be prompted to intervene by excesses. And Generals Tolimir and Gvero are particularly attuned to this. Again, they are the generals next to General Mladic who most interact with the international community, most have their eyes on the military political developments across the world. And please note, Your Honours, how quickly this happens. Basically within half an hour of Krstic's interim combat report, Tolimir is issued this critical communication to Karadzic, Krstic, and Gvero. There's none of this fog of war nonsense that he's been throwing at the UNPROFOR generals for two days. No, let me call you back in 40 minutes, General Krstic, Mr. President, because I don't know what's happening in the field. This document, the evidence will show, is compelling evidence that General Tolimir knew all along, during his conversations with Nicolai and Janvier, of what was developing on the battlefront in Srebrenica. When the crucial time came to make this pivotal decision, General Tolimir was able to move quickly. He was sufficiently informed, he had the knowledge he needed, he was secure that this proposal from General Krstic was militarily sound, and he was part of that proposal and approval process. Now, the attack, not surprisingly, continues. This decisive attack to take the town gets underway and stays underway. You'll see a conversation the next morning between General Mladic and General Janvier, again it's the same old song. I don't know what the picture is. I have to go down to the spot. I need to call you back. I have to talk to my subordinate commanders. The Muslims are attacking. We're not attacking anybody. Whether it's General Tolimir, General Gvero, General Mladic, it's the same script. And we see on the 10th more misery, more civilian victims. The number of casualties and wounded is increasing. UN APCs are being damaged. When they sent out a recovery vehicle, when the UN sent out a recovery vehicle, the recovery vehicle got fired on by the VRS. This report at about 1100 hours: "Two heavy shells probably 150-millimetre artillery shells hit the direct surrounding of the hospital at 1100 hours. All the windows are smashed and shrapnel had showered the walls and rooms of the hospital. The surgery is very difficult to proceed." It looks as if the VRS are now targeting the hospital and the surroundings. And the shelling continues and continues. And from what the UNMOs were seeing, they estimated that the situation was going to get worse and that it was getting worse. And you'll hear more and see more reports like this. Peacekeepers seeing villages being burned to the south of the enclave. And again, during this period when the blocking positions are being -- have been set up, these UN peacekeepers are being fired on. You'll hear testimony from these DutchBat officers; for example, an officer named Egbers that at first he couldn't tell whether his APC was actually being targeted or whether it was just close fire or whether they were firing at something that was close to his APC. But when he moved his APC, the shelling followed, and when he returned to his prior position, the shelling followed him back. You'll hear that all the shelling was causing, as the VRS had intended, this -- the population to withdraw to the centre of town. Colonel Franken recalled that there was massive shelling on the 10th and he ordered his peacekeepers to stop counting the shells. And what happens at this point was the minimal resistance that was left from some of the Muslim fighters collapsed, leaving the DutchBat positions completely exposed, which ones that were left at that point. So that evening we see another intercept 2015, again between Generals Janvier and Tolimir. And we see P here is the interpreter, the intermediary for General Janvier. T is Tolimir. So General Janvier is saying that -- to Tolimir that: "Your units are attacking our soldiers." Tolimir says: "I don't have such information. I'll try to reach them by phone to check. I don't believe our soldiers are attacking your soldiers since they have been avoiding it up to now." That's just a lie. Again, denying that he has such information. He's going to check with his commander: "He hasn't reported to me that there was any attack." Of course there was an attack. General Tolimir was instrumental in getting that attack approved at the highest levels. Again, General Tolimir doing what he can just to get the UN off his back. I'll establish contact, try to prevent a conflict situation. Janvier's insistent: "He says to stop and secondly that they have to withdraw where they were before." General Tolimir says: I understand perfectly. Give him my regards. And I'm going to check, call me back, 20 to 30 minutes. And as you can see here, General Janvier knows that he's getting the runaround. And he says: "As far as I understand, you are very talkative and you are not capable of doing anything else." General Tolimir undeterred: "I understood you, and I will check the information." You'll see other conversations -- in fact, two other conversations later that night between General Tolimir and General Janvier along the same lines. In one of them General Tolimir claims that he has called a cease-fire or called a halt to the attack and claims that the UNPROFOR soldiers were being forced by the Muslims to fire on the Serbs. He says he'd be happy to meet with General Gobillard the next day, the 11th of July, in Sarajevo, but he said he needs to -- he needs more time. He needs to get more information. He says the Muslims have planted many rumours about the situation in the field. He denies again that the VRS is attacking. He says it might be the Muslims, and suggests that Janvier speak with Mladic in the morning. So by the 11th of July, the town of Srebrenica was in utter chaos. People were terrified. They were collecting around the Bravo Company compound, the UN compound down there. And you'll hear that a shell fell on that compound, causing casualties, killing civilians. And then you'll hear testimony about how it reached a point where the civilians simply couldn't take it anymore. They had been shelled and shelled and shelled, compressed into this town and they had nowhere to go but out. And so they decided to flee, if you remember, Bravo Company in Srebrenica town is to the south of Charlie Company, which was the compound in Potocari. So these civilians decide to try to make it to some place safer. So they proceed on foot. A huge column of people, women, children, elderly, wounded, grabbing whatever they can, in some cases nothing, just their lives, and they try to make it up to Potocari to safety. You'll hear that the UN, when they saw this happening, did their best to help. They sent trucks down. The UN peacekeepers that were in Srebrenica were told to assist and help escort. You'll hear from Colonel Kingori and other DutchBat officers how the shelling then proceeded to, in a way, funnel them out. It tracked this column of mostly civilians up towards Potocari, pushing them further up towards Potocari. You'll hear that the column itself was not attacked, but that the shells were falling on either side and that people understood, they could tell that they were being pushed, pushed up to the Potocari compound. And at first the civilians were placed in the compound, but once that got too full up in Potocari they began to fill abandoned factories and other sites just to the south of the compound. You'll hear about the terror of these people as they arrived, of their children screaming, awaiting some measure of safety, gathered in the open in these factory compound sites just south of the UN compound. And you'll hear that the close air support finally was delivered in the afternoon of 11 of July. You'll hear that that close air support was immediately followed by death threats from the VRS. You'll hear that using a radio in one of the captured APCs, the Serbs sent a message from one of these or through one of these peacekeepers that they had held in Bratunac back to the compound in Potocari: We will kill your men, your peacekeepers, if the close air support continues. And they also threatened to shell the compound and the area around it where the civilians were if the close air support did not stop. Now, you'll hear that Colonel Franken, the DutchBat deputy commander, at the time he was a major, you'll hear him say that he didn't take the threat to kill the UN hostages that seriously; but he did take the VRS threat to shell the civilians very seriously because he'd seen it done before. That's what had been happening the entire time, and he fully believed that the VRS was capable, 100 per cent capable, of carrying out its threat. Now, you'll see that there is evidence to suggest that General Tolimir is not in the Main Staff command post on the 11th of July at this time. It's General Gvero who has now stepped in to be the main officer there. And you'll see conversations again between General Nicolai and Gvero and General Gobillard and Gvero, where this mantra is repeated. This is General Gvero speaking, but it could have just easily been Tolimir. It's the same words: We have nothing to halt. We never did that at all. We're not shelling UN positions, we're not targeting the civilian population. And then just like the threat that had been radioed in, General Gvero who's just a little more delicate tells General Nicolai: "In case General Nicolai doesn't order the bombing to stop," that's the close air support, "and doesn't withdraw NATO airplanes, he will have personal responsibility for further developments and for destiny of all people in the area." And you'll hear from General Nicolai that he knew what that meant and he took that threat seriously again, repeating the threat to bomb everybody if the UN got in the way with the only weapon it had. You'll hear that he and General Gobillard because they took that threat seriously, they called off the air support and that was it. And again General Gvero tells General Nicolai, it's just Muslim propaganda. Now, far from being deterred by the use of the UN air power, you'll see, the evidence will show, that the VRS pressed its attack even more. And we have General Gvero now communicating directly with President Karadzic, just like the evidence indicates that General Tolimir was in direct contact with General Karadzic -- President Karadzic on the night of the 9th of July. We have an intercept here between General Gvero and President Karadzic. "I just talked to that General Nicolai ... he wants -- he says, stop attacking the UN. I hold him that his information is probably from the Muslims and that we haven't been attacking the UN. I'm asking him to stop the operation immediately and get those planes out of the sky." That's what they're worried about, those planes: "Everything is going according to plan, don't worry." That's General Gvero to President Karadzic: "Yes, yes, we'll try because they are a tremendous hindrance." It's just like General Tolimir, telling Krstic and Zivanovic on the 9th of July: I'll take care of tying up the UN. That will allow you to work according to plan. A few minutes later General Gvero again, in direct contact with President Karadzic. He's reporting: "President, Serbian Silver," that no doubt refers to the old silver mines for which Srebrenica is named, "the Serbian church, the Serbian flag." We see the critical communication link that the VRS Main Staff was to President Karadzic, and here the intercept operator, the Muslim army intercept operator, notes that: "General Gvero is the only one present today at the Main Staff." He calls it the Supreme Command headquarters, but you'll hear that he's talking about the Main Staff. And you'll hear that the lies just continue seamlessly. General Gobillard now gets on the phone with General Gvero, again denying, just like General Tolimir did, that UN members had been shot at, they were shot at by the Muslims. Our troops didn't open fire: "The UN has never been and I hope never will be our enemy. "Nor are civilians in that region our enemies, and we'll do everything in our power to protect them. "We have not attacked ... "The refugees who come over to our side will be totally safe. We will protect those civilians ..." Now, you'll see a document that's issued by General Gvero later that night pretty soon after some of these conversations, and again this is of a piece with the other instructions to be careful with UNPROFOR, obey the Geneva Conventions. General Gvero notes that: "In relation to the total situation of the enclave of Srebrenica, the monitoring of reactions from UNPROFOR representatives and the world public opinion indicates that the attitude of the VRS personnel towards UNPROFOR personnel and units in the area of Srebrenica is in the focus of attention." So he orders the troops: Don't screw it up. It's in our hands. Don't get the international community involved. Remember that language from Directive 7: Do it unobtrusively, that's how we're going to do it, avoid international condemnation. They knew how far they could go when the world was watching. And the evidence will show that these threats, the delay, the false statements, the lies from Generals Tolimir and Gvero directly impeded the UN's ability to react to this military attack. It retarded their decision-making. It allowed them to complete the plan. And again, the UNMOs are reporting that as these refugees are streaming in, the shelling of the town has been going on despite the air-strikes. He refers to the end of this excerpt: "The latest ultimatum given by the VRS is that if the air-strikes continue everything inside the enclave will be bombed including UNPROFOR and other UN organisations." You can't believe a word Generals Tolimir, Gvero, Mladic say when they're speaking to the UN. That's what the evidence is going to show. References to the Geneva Conventions. The number of wounded is growing, severely wounded is growing, they don't have enough medicines because of the restrictions. We see how Directive 7 plays a tragic part, even at the very end of the life of the enclave, its final hours. The evidence will show that the Srebrenica enclave fell in the afternoon of 11 July, and you'll see video of General Mladic accompanied by some of his main officers, Generals Zivanovic, General Krstic. You'll see the chief of security, Vujadin Popovic, who you've heard about and you'll hear a lot more about in a moment, accompanying him from the Drina Corps. You'll see the 10th Sabotage Detachment commander, Milorad Pelemis, all of them taking this triumphant walk through the empty streets of Srebrenica town. And to give you an idea of what was to come, I want to play a little piece of video and you'll see General Mladic turning to the camera and saying what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The time has come to take revenge on the Turks in this region. I see we're about a minute away from the break, Mr. President, if I could break now, this would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Thayer. Could you perhaps indicate if you will be able to conclude your opening statement by the end of the -- today's sitting?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is my intention, Mr. President, and I will do everything I can to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should be aware of the fact that we -- there is no courtroom available for another sitting this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood. I will comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We'll have a break now and resume five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Srebrenica Muslims took two courses of action at this point. We have the one group of tens of thousands of women, children, some military-aged men, elderly, who had fled to the UNPROFOR compound in Potocari, seeking refuge there, and they stayed there from the 11th through the 13th. A second group of approximately 15.000 Muslim men and boys with some women gathered in the village of Susnjari, and then during the evening of 11 July began to flee on foot to the north-west in a huge column using an old smuggling route. About a third of this column was armed, and that armed group was towards the front. The rest were unarmed military personnel, civilians, and some women and children. You'll hear and you'll see the video of the Hotel Fontana meetings. There were three of these meetings. The first two occurred on the night of the 11th. I won't go into too much detail about those. What's important to note now is that General Tolimir had his men on the ground at these meetings. You may recall back when we were talking about the intelligence administration, I mentioned a Colonel Radoslav Jankovic. He is present for these meetings. He is sitting next to Mladic. Also present is Svetozar Kosoric, who is the Drina Corps intelligence chief. He is present as well. You'll hear about the atmosphere of fear and control, intimidation that Mladic created during these meetings. You'll hear that at the second meeting that a window was opened so that everybody gathered could hear the screams of a pig being slaughtered. Mladic displays the broken sign of the Srebrenica town hall. He told a Muslim representative that had been essentially picked out of the crowd at Mladic's direction when he said, "I want to speak with some representative of the Muslim population," he told that man, a man named Nesib Mandzic, and I quote: "I need to have a clear position of the representatives of your people on whether you want to survive, stay, or vanish." And he told Mr. Mandzic that the future of your people is in your hands." That was the second Hotel Fontana meeting, and he demanded that UNPROFOR and Mandzic bring more high-level, more responsible - as he saw it - representatives. And I quote again: " ... with whom I can discuss the salvation of your people and save your people from destruction." You'll see that Mladic was, as he ought to have been, concerned about the number of military-aged men in the area, particularly in Potocari. And you'll hear that he was in fact receiving information that night that over a thousand military-aged men were among the tens of thousands of refugees at the base in Potocari. So that is very much on General Mladic's mind, starting in the evening of the 11th of July. You'll also hear that in that compound in Potocari those terrified, exhausted, desperate civilians, the conditions were horrendous and were getting worse. You'll hear that there was suicide, attempted suicide. There was no access to basic toilet facilities, minimal food. And you'll hear that the civilians were preyed upon, singled out for terrorisation and intimidation, and opportunistic murders as well. And this happened between the 12th -- from the 11th through the 13th. So by the morning of the 12th there are about 30.000-plus refugees at the Potocari compound, and the question any intelligence officer worth his or her salt should be asking and in fact were asking at the time is: Where are the Muslim men? Where are the military-aged of men? Where is the 28th Division? And again, Mladic had received information already that there were 1200 to 1500 able-bodied men in Potocari. That information was sent up the intelligence chain, as we call it, the intelligence professional chain of command. Mladic had that information. And certainly General Tolimir, and as you'll see from the documents, was receiving that information as well. The third Hotel Fontana meeting you'll also see the addition, in addition to General Tolimir's men, Jankovic and Kosoric, you'll see the Drina Corps security chief, Vujadin Popovic, and you'll see Lieutenant-Colonel Milutinovic, the head of the Main Staff press centre there as well. Mladic repeats his threat to survive or disappear, and he makes it a point of saying, and I quote: "You may choose to stay in the territory or, if you wish, go wherever you want. The wish of every individual will be observed no matter how many of you there are. You can choose to stay or you can choose to leave. Just express your wish." That's what he says on camera, when he knows that they're making propaganda. And one thing he also said at this meeting, which notably is not filmed or was filmed and then later cut, was that he announced that all the men between the ages of 16 and 60 would be separated, purportedly so that they could be screened for war crimes. Now, this is a significant statement on his -- on General Mladic's part. And as the evidence will show, Your Honours, there was no screening. There was only separations. All of the men between the ages of 16 and 60, including many who were 12 to 15 and over 60, were separated. And you'll see that while this third Fontana meeting on the morning of the 12th is going on, there is this massive logistical operation conducted by the Drina Corps and the Main Staff, the Ministry of Defence, civilian authorities, to mobilise buses, trucks, fuel, personnel to transport these Muslims out of Potocari, to get them out of there. That's all going on while this is happening. The orders went out first thing in the morning before Mladic sat down at this third meeting. What you're seeing is a photograph taken before this third Fontana meeting. On the far left is Momir Nikolic, the Bratunac Brigade chief of intelligence and security. Next, moving left to right, is Radoslav Jankovic, General Tolimir's intelligence officer from the Main Staff who was at all these meetings. In the doorway is a body-guard of General Mladic, and on the far right is Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic, the Drina Corps security chief. These are General Tolimir's of men. This is a still from the third Fontana meeting. I want to call your attention to the man in the uniform at the far right at the end of the table with the big prominent moustache. That is Svetozar Kosoric, the Drina Corps chief of intelligence. Witnesses and videotape will place all of these men in Potocari during the separations and the forcible transfer. They were there doing their jobs, collecting information and intelligence, assessing the security situation, sending that information up their chain. And the evidence will show, Your Honours, that ultimately they were there to organise and oversee the expulsion of the Muslim women, children, and elderly; the detention of the men that were being culled out of the crowd in Potocari; and the operation to capture, detain, and execute the Muslim men and boys that were fleeing in the column. Now, Momir Nikolic will tell you that before this third Hotel Fontana meeting, Vujadin Popovic told him in the presence of Kosoric that, and I quote: "All the balija have to be killed." And you'll hear that "balija" is a particularly offensive epithet used against Muslims. There was a lot of name-calling, you'll hear, during the war by both sides. You'll see the word "Turk" used in documents a lot. Sometimes "potorice" refers to Slavs who converted to Islam. But "balija" was an exceptionally vile term which was used, and you won't see it as frequently as these other terms in the documents as much as you'll see "Turk," for example, but you'll see it used particularly commonly by the security organ and you'll see it used by General Tolimir himself. So at this meeting between Nikolic and Popovic before the third Hotel Fontana meeting, in the presence of Kosoric, after Popovic says that all the Muslims are going to be killed, Nikolic suggests some detention sites and some execution sites around the Bratunac area. Meanwhile what's happening is Serb forces have gathered, both to the north of the enclave from the Bratunac area and they're still at the south of the enclave where they've been pressing that attack the entire time. And they proceed in an organised fashion to finally enter Potocari and take over the entire area. And you'll hear testimony about this organised movement in attack formation, soldiers setting houses on fire, some with dogs entering the houses, cleaning -- cleansing the houses, the houses bursting into flames. As they proceed down that main road that runs north-south right in front of the DutchBat compound in Potocari. They proceed on either side and some right down the main road. And you'll see video of the soldiers entering Potocari. And pay attention, please, you'll see at one point a MUP Special Police brigade commander, a man with very noticeable sun glasses, moustache, his nickname is Stalin, his name is Dusko Jevic, and you'll see how interested he is in where are the military-aged men. And, Your Honours, the Prosecution's case is that by this time General Mladic has made the decision that the men and boys of Srebrenica are going to be murdered. And you'll see video, again taken for propaganda purposes, of General Mladic talking to the miserable refugees, candy being handed out. You'll see General Mladic making a big show of telling them they have nothing to fear, patting children on the head, assuring them that they're free to stay if they wish, but again what he says and what he means and what he does are a different thing entirely. This is an intercept captured at 1250 hours on the 12th between General Mladic and an unknown individual. He's asking: "Have these buses and trucks left?" He's told they have. "When? "Ten minutes ago." And he says: "Good, excellent. Continue to monitor the situation. Don't let small groups of them sneak in. They've all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all - those who want to and those who don't want to." Nothing was going to interfere with the VRS plan to move the Muslim population out completely. This is a still picture of what part of the crowd looked like that day. What then got underway, Your Honours, was an organised and systematic separation of the men from their families and the expulsion of the women, children, and elderly. People who didn't want to be separated from their families or board the buses were forced to. You'll hear evidence about the Serbs pushing and kicking, beating with rifle-butts, verbally abusing, spitting on people to get them to the buses which were then overfilled. And you'll hear that the Serb forces separated out the men of this large crowd, which was cordoned off by Dutch peacekeepers. You'll hear that they separated men out and would allow groups of women and children and elderly to pass up next to the column of buses that had parked, and you'll hear that if a man, a male, military-aged or not, youngsters, elderly men, will be plucked out of that group that had managed to make it towards the buses. And you'll hear that if a man was lucky enough to make it on to a bus, the buses were stopped at check-points and searched, and the men were taken off the buses along the route. They were lucky to make it through that, when the buses disembarked, men were separated at that point, and you'll hear testimony about those men being taken away and executed. The separations were marked by brutality and scenes of unbearable distress and heart-break. And you'll hear testimony from some of these survivors themselves about that. The men who were separated were taken to detention homes near the UN compound, an unfinished house, another house you'll hear referred to as the white house. You'll hear Dutch peacekeepers who wanted to find out what was going on in that white house were turned away at gunpoint, threatened, guns placed inside their mouths if they tried to find out what was going on. And critically for our purposes you'll hear that before going into the white house those men were forced to throw down their belongings and, in particular, their identification documents. All of these IDs and belongings formed a big pile in front of the white house you'll hear. You might hear some evidence about a list of war criminals, of Muslim war criminals that the Serbs had put together and that was circulating, but the evidence will show it's beyond dispute that there was no process of determining identities of those separated men. How could they when the identification documents were sitting in a pile in front of the white house? There were no lists made of prisoners, no food given, no access to sanitation or medical aid; in other words, there was no life support because these men were condemned to die. This is compelling evidence that as early as 12 July these men were never going to be exchanged, interrogated, awaiting POW change-over; they were going to be killed. The men from the white house were then bussed to Bratunac, where they either stayed inside the buses or were placed in various buildings in and around Bratunac, such as the Vuk Karadzic school you'll hear about and a couple of buildings in that complex. They were placed out of sight. And wherever they were, they were preyed upon, more fell to opportunistic murders, and again no life support. I'd like to show you a video-clip now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You see these men not of military age. If you watch the clip again, you'll see them being directed in a particular direction. The Prosecution will introduce evidence of nearly 1.000 men aged 61 or older and boys under the age of 16 recovered from mass graves, a damning testament to the lack of screening and a clear plan to kill as many men and boys as they thought they could. And you'll hear that in Potocari on the late afternoon of the 12th that Serb forces began systematically stopping and stripping peacekeepers of their equipment. In the words of Colonel Franken, taking away their eyes and ears, preventing the DutchBat officers from being witnesses to what was going on, preventing them from escorting the buses. And of course General Tolimir has his eyes and ears on the ground, that's why he has Jankovic, Kosoric, and Popovic, and he's getting regular reports, and they're pushing that information up to him. And I'd like to turn now to some of these reports emanating by General Tolimir through his intelligence and security command chain. The first document we're going to look at here is from Major Pavle Golic. He is a Drina Corps intelligence officer, an assistant to Kosoric, the gentleman with the big moustache that you saw from the Hotel Fontana. He's relaying information from a captured soldier that there's a large group. Right now their information is only that it's a thousand strong, including soldiers, women and children. And you'll see that this is going to General Tolimir's sector, and specifically to the intelligence administration, which means Colonel Salapura. Golic notes that: "Upon reaching the general area of Konjevic Polje and Cerska, he would most probably ask the UN for protection," he's referring to one of the leaders, one of the military leaders that's part of this column. So the intelligence organ is proposing that ambushes be set up, that the Drina Corps duty officer and the operations officer, key officers being made aware of the situation and that the MUP is notified. And again, this is a good example of how a professional, disciplined army works and this is -- you'll see the area in Konjevic Polje that General Tolimir knew all about and ordered MUP forces to -- I should say proposed MUP forces to, but that was fully accepted and implemented by President Karadzic. Now, the next document we're going to look at that goes out that same night, and you'll see that these reports run in sequence. This is from the Drina Corps command under the heading of the intelligence department. And you'll see that this is type signed by General Tolimir. So this suggests that he is at the Drina Corps command, not at the Main Staff. He's where the action is. He sends it to all the appropriate people who need to know, the MUP, state security, Popovic, Krstic personally at the IKM. And he's relaying information from a captured prisoner. And he says: "On the basis of this interview, it can be concluded that the civilians ... have set off ... to seek refuge in Potocari," which is correct, "while the armed formations ... are trying a break through," also correct.
