If there's something in writing, it's going to be in code or encrypted, and you're going to see a few examples that are owing to sheer sloppiness or stupidity or pure arrogance where there are references after the fact to the executions, but you're not going to see General Tolimir slip up like that. Now, on the 16th or the night of the 15th the burials are continuing in Orahovac, executions in Petkovci continue at the dam, Kozluk, and we just heard the conversation where Beara's trying to get men to finish this job up here. It's simply impossible, you'll see from the evidence, that General Tolimir, the chief of intelligence and security for the entire army, was not fully aware of the situation; that Beara was not consulting with him, his immediate superior; that Tolimir was not active in formulating the solution. He had to have been part of finding that solution for Beara's 3500 parcels. The 10th Sabotage Unit just doesn't get into a van itself and drive all the way up to Pilica. Krstic couldn't do it, Beara couldn't do it by himself. So when we get to the 16th of July, we have another intercept. This is involving a Colonel Cerovic who is the morale officer of the Drina Corps and he is engaged in this process. He is saying triage has to be done on the prisoners, he says it twice. And then the other participant says: "Beara is right here by me. "All right. Give me Beara. "Go ahead. "Yes? "Ljubo. "I hear you." Cerovic identifies himself. He says: "Trkula," that's a Main Staff colonel, chief of the armoured services, "was here with me just now and he was looking for you ... "He told me he got instructions from above ... "To do triage ..." And then Beara says: "I don't want to talk about it on the phone." We know that triage means only one thing and it has nothing to do with screening the wounded, so that all the prisoners who were left wind up dead. And General Tolimir, although he's down in the Zepa area, Mladic being buoyed by the success of Srebrenica decides to turn directly to taking Zepa, and he sends General Tolimir down there to implement that order. We see an intercept just an hour before this last intercept that we saw where triage is being ordered from a Main Staff -- through a Main Staff officer to Beara. We see in this intercept Toso and Mico. That's General Tolimir, and you'll hear that Mico is General Miletic. Tolimir is saying that he can be contacted through Uran, that's the code-name for the forward command post of the Drina Corps, General Krstic. "One of his lines isn't secure," so he's saying this is how I can get secure communications. "And tell Pepo." You'll hear Pepo is Petar Salapura. "If you need to get ahold of me, this is how you can do it." And of course he's already talking to the Main Staff. He's just making sure that there is a secure and reliable way to continue doing that, because he's with Krstic. Tolimir says: "I've just sent a telegram." And then he says two telegrams urgently he just sent. And you see they make arrangements to make sure that these communications continue. So we know that General Tolimir is in communications. He has options that he's exercising about how to do that with the Main Staff, Tolimir from one end, Beara from the other, the Main Staff in the middle, relaying the information. And you'll see that on the 16th you'll hear testimony from a 10th Sabotage Member, Drazen Erdemovic. You'll hear from him that his platoon went up that morning on the 16th. He sees an officer matching Beara's description there and they do their work. You'll hear from another 10th Sabotage soldier who says that Dragomir Pecanac, another Main Staff officer under General Tolimir's command, arrived and made arrangements to bring that group in a van up to the Branjevo area. Pecanac will be a figure to watch when we turn to the Zepa operation shortly. And you'll hear testimony about when the killing at the Branjevo farm was finished, there were still over 500 prisoners left in the cultural centre in Pilica. You'll hear testimony that that execution was conduct by Bratunac Brigade members. And of course this burial operation -- this murder operation required the burial of the bodies to conceal the crime. This is an intercept from that day, the 16th in the afternoon, Basevic is a Drina Corps officer, rear services type. "The guys at Zlatar didn't understand well, I asked for the duty officer, you know?" Zlatar is the code-name for the Drina Corps. "Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic is here at Palma," again Palma is the Zvornik Brigade. He repeats it. "Popovic is at Palma. "500 litres of D2," that's diesel fuel, "are urgently being asked for him or else the work he's doing will stop." That work is finishing the execution job, burying the bodies of the Branjevo farm. And then you'll see that Golic is contacted, the intelligence officer. "Pop just called me and told me to contact you. 500 litres of D2 have to be sent to him immediately, otherwise his work will stop." Like at the other sites you'll see evidence of the engineering equipment and the manpower and the fuel and all of the mechanics of finishing up this job. And you'll see again how in communication General Tolimir is throughout this entire period. This is an intercept from the 16th, that afternoon while the killings are underway in Branjevo. This is an intercept with General Mladic. Mladic says: " ... I've just sent a telegram to Toso ... the President called a short while ago and said that he had been informed by Karisik," that's a Ministry of Interior official, "that Pandurevic," he's the Zvornik Brigade commander, "has arranged passage for the Muslims over to that territory. Since I have no communication with him, I asked the duty officer to urgently connect me with him, to send me a telegram with that information and not to do anything without authorisation until he receives our answer." So there's always a way to get in contact with General Tolimir and vice versa and here we have General Mladic doing so. And this issue that he's talking about is this column had finally overrun some of the defence lines of the Zvornik Brigade and was presenting a very grave threat to the lives of the Serb soldiers that were manning those trenches and many had been killed, and you'll hear that the Zvornik Brigade commander made the decision to open up a corridor for a limited period of time to allow the remnants of the column, this portion of the column that was still moving, to cross into free territory, to save further Zvornik Brigade soldiers' lives because the Muslims were so desperate they had overrun, literally overruned the positions and turned the Serbs guns, anti-aircraft guns back on them. It was a matter of grave concern to the Main Staff. You'll hear that General Miletic was all over it. They sent three Main Staff colonels to investigate it, so of course General Tolimir is going to know about this. We see that from this intercept here. I see that we've arrived at the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. We will have only 20-minutes' break, to give you the opportunity to finish your opening statement today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, you've heard some reference throughout my opening so far to a duty officer's notebook. That's what this is. It was seized, taken from the Zvornik Brigade, passed into the hands of the OTP. What it is is it's an informal notebook kept by the duty operations officer at the Zvornik Brigade. In it, the duty operations officer jotted down calls that were coming in, inquiries, requests, orders, instructions, information to pass on from one place to the other from the battalions that were subordinate to the Zvornik Brigade and from superior commands. You'll be able to see the original if you wish to during the trial. It covers the period of the murder operation, and it is a diary of death. What you're seeing on your screen are just some selections from this notebook. Just focusing on General Tolimir's direct subordinate Beara and other members of the security organs, 13 July. President of the municipality asking for a flat-bed trailer and a bulldozer, Colonel Beara directly involved with this. This is on the 13th. "14 July, Colonel Salapura called - Drago," that's Drago Nikolic, Zvornik Brigade security officer "and Beara are to report to Golic," Golic being the Drina Corps intelligence officer. And here we have Colonel Salapura, again the Main Staff chief of intelligence calling into the Zvornik Brigade duty operations officer to make sure this message gets conveyed. 1500 hours - Colonel Beara is coming in order to ..." and you see the names of those execution sites; Orahovac spelled incorrectly here, probably quickly, Petkovci, Rocevic, Pilica. Same day, a little later: "Beara to call 155," that's the Main Staff centre operations. "From Beara - Drago to report Mane - Djukici." You'll hear evidence that that is actually Mane Djuric, a MUP officer. "0900 Beara is coming," clearing referring to the next morning Beara is coming to the Zvornik Brigade command. The next day, 15 July: "Communicate to Popovic that his proposal has been approved." Again, Popovic is out in the field, as the evidence will show, at these sites. And the operations officer at the Zvornik Brigade command is transmitting these messages back and forth. 15 July: "Drago and Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic," again the Drina Corps chief of security, "are to report to Major Golic early in the morning," making sure that this information is flowing up to where it needs to go and where it needs to go is General Tolimir. 16 July: "0855 hours Golic asked Popovic to call him and said that he can forget what he asked for and what he wrote about. He knows what he is supposed to do according to agreed procedure (Boss from Panorama 01)." Panorama being the Main Staff. "Message conveyed to Popovic at 0910 hours." And again: "Beara to call Panorama 155, 0930 hours. "At 1115 hours. It was reported from Zlatar," that's the Drina Corps, "that a triage of wounded and prisoners must be carried out (this was reported to Beara)." You saw the intercept yourselves just a few minutes ago, Your Honours, and it was recorded in this notebook, that was Colonel Cerovic calling from the Drina Corps saying the triage had to be done. And those are those prisoners that are going to be executed by the 10th Sabotage Detachment at Branjevo: "1400 hours Popovic requested a bus with a full tank and 500 litres of D2." Again, that's an intercept you saw, or his work will stop. Your Honours, the evidence will show that each of these killing sites was uniquely horrible, but there are certain commonalities among them. Prisoners were consistently stripped of their belongings, the IDs were piled in front of these detention sites so there was no screening to be done. There were robbed, they were not given any life support, they were beaten, verbally abused. You need to stand a little bit at a distance really to see what was required to complete this plan, to comprehend its enormity. It is staggering in its degree of co-ordination and planning. You needed to have co-ordination among the VRS units with MUP, civilian structures, you had to identify the detention centres close to the execution sites, you had to issue, transmit, disseminate the orders to make sure they are being followed up on, so you have Beara and Popovic and Momir Nikolic paying all their visits. You have to move, detain, murder, and bury all of these prisoners, which requires getting the vehicles and the thousands of litres of scarce fuel to transport them. You need personnel to do all that, to secure every one of those locations in that entire process. You have to secure the routes, as we heard. You have to make blindfolds and ligatures. You have to actually assemble the killing squads. You have to direct them. You have to arm them. You have to find officers who are going to be willing to make sure that this job gets done. A lot of these shooters were reserve officers. As I said, the farmer soldiers. So you need people to manage the executioners' will to keep killing, and you need to manage the managers. And that was General Tolimir. You heard about all the earth-moving equipment. You'll see evidence of that, and that all required again not just the security organs but the commanders and all of their resources and authorisation for their men and materiel to be used. This was systematic, organised mass murder, and the evidence will show that it was genocide. No men were meant to get out alive. Men were separated out of the crowd, as I said before, in Potocari, they were separated every step of the way. They didn't want to miss a one. And in the process there was only utter dehumanisation. The evidence will show that these men were condemned to die. You will hear evidence that they were told they wouldn't need their IDs any longer where you're going, you're not going to need that back-pack where you're going. You've already heard about the old men and young boys in those graves. You'll heard about boys, prisoners, who were used to fetch water at a couple of locations, in each case those boys didn't make it. They didn't have a chance. They too were condemned to die. This is all evidence of the genocidal nature of this plan. What we'll see over the days and weeks following the organised mass executions is that whenever the VRS or MUP forces scouring the woods and hills found some lost Muslims still trying to make it back to safe territory, if they thought they could get away with it they executed them. You see this at Nezuk, Snagovo, you see it on the Skorpions' video. You see prisoners brought back from Serbia through the Bratunac Brigade and delivered to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic at Bisina where they too were executed by the 10th Sabotage Detachment. That can only be done with General Tolimir's authorisation. You will see evidence that even four survivors of the Branjevo executions, four guys that made it got captured again. They didn't make it the second time. Again, if they thought they could get away with it, the Serb soldiers killed anybody they could get their hands on. Unless in very specific circumstances there was the idea that a small amount might be saved for an execution, for an exchange, beg your pardon. You might hear a little bit of evidence about that. That is the extreme exception. This is an intercept from the next day, 17th of July, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic referring to the burials at Branjevo: "The job is done ... everything's been brought to an end, no problems. ... basically it all gets an A ... the grade is an A." You'll hear from the reserve soldiers that had the gruesome task of transporting those bodies from the Pilica Dom to the Branjevo farm to be buried. You'll note that this is at 1622 on the 17th, and you'll see an intercept from 1652. To save some time I won't put it up right now. It's Miletic, Mico, and Toso, General Tolimir, 17 of July. You'll see them talking about a meeting that General Tolimir needs to go to. Again, General Tolimir always in contact, always in the know because it was his job to know. And you're also going to hear that by this time Potocari is empty. All that's left are DutchBat soldiers, some MSF, Doctors Without Borders staff, and local employees, Muslims. UNHCR had a couple of people there and they were wounded, wounded Muslim men. And since you'll hear that UNPROFOR had made a list, MSF had made a list of these wounded men, they were known to the international community. And ICRC and UNHCR was pressing to visit these prisoners as well as the prisoners that they thought had been taken after the fall of Srebrenica and that they didn't know had been already executed and buried. So you see time and again ICRC and General Smith asking for access to the prisoners who were dead. So General Tolimir needs to know what to do about these wounded. Even under ordinary circumstances he would need to know. If you have the ICRC asking to transfer these people, General Tolimir needs to know about these prisoners because he needs to know if they are of intelligence value, if there are soldiers hidden among them, high-level officers. But of course he needs to know now because he knows that the whole area from Kravica all the way up to Pilica that you saw on that map is one big crime scene. And he's got to handle this very carefully, these wounded. So you'll see reports and intercepts back and forth between Colonel Jankovic, who's still in Bratunac, who's reporting to General Tolimir about what's been happening with these wounded; and you'll see, for example, here in this intercept on the 17th a caller is telling Jankovic that Miletic said that Jankovic should put whatever he's concerned about in code, in a coded telegram, and send it to Tolimir. So again, we know that General Tolimir is able to receive encrypted communications. Again, you're not going to see him make the mistake of talking stupidly on an open line. And here's a reference to Tolimir having to get together with Mladic and make a decision about what to do with these people. Are they going to be set free, are they going to be detained? Are they going to be sent to a prison? Are they going to be isolated and squirrelled away and then executed? What's the plan going to be? We see in connection with the movement of the wounded, and you'll hear that most of the severely wounded were freed to go to Tuzla. Twenty-two lightly wounded were taken to a prison in Batkovic on the 18th. But we'll see General Miletic in connection with the movement of some of these wounded directing the Bratunac Brigade, in particular the security organs, to constantly monitor the NGO's activities. Must not be allowed to go anywhere on their own, must restrict their movement, be polite. Again, there's always that attention to being unobtrusive, don't push too far; in other words, though, the security organs must direct their movement. And again that's because General Miletic knows, General Tolimir knows, it's a crime scene. And Miletic isn't just inserting this language because he thinks it's a good idea on his own; he's doing that in consultation with General Tolimir and his organs. No one's going to tell these guys like Momir Nikolic other than his own commander, no one's going to tell the security guys what to do other than General Tolimir. A message like that coming from the Main Staff isn't coming just from General Miletic. We'll see other intercepts, Your Honours, that show that units are waiting for General Tolimir's decisions regarding these wounded. We have here again Colonel Jankovic writing to General Tolimir, talking about the evacuations of the wounded. This is on the 18th. He's writing from the brigade command of the Bratunac Brigade. And then he asks: "Will you please take a stand. Tell me what stand to take, actually, in terms of the authorisation for... these MSF employees and the local staff," the Muslim men who are employed by MSF. What do we do with them? Jankovic is saying: It's my opinion they shouldn't be held. Karadzic wanted them abolished. I don't think they should be held, and he's writing to Tolimir to ask what to do. And again you remember the night before Jankovic was told: Send something to Tolimir. And you'll see later that night Jankovic saying, "I sent you a paper, I'm sending you a paper." And he asks if Toso is there and he'll get it when he arrives. Now, the next day there's an intercept between, again, Colonel Jankovic and Milos Djurdjic, a Main Staff officer, who was involved in the convoy-approval procedure, but he's in the Main Staff and is taking this call with Jankovic. Jankovic essentially is saying: Look, I've got these MSF local staff. They're Muslim, they're Muslim men and they're of military age. And he's told that there's permission from the government to let them go. There's a list. MSF has a list of these men. They are known to the international community. Djurdjic says: "Yes, I know, I can see the names," and then he starts reading these Muslim men's names. "2, 4, 6, 7 men." They've got permission. But Djurdjic says: " ... but you know what the procedure -- you know that procedure you too took part in ..." Djurdjic repeats: "The procedure is such, God damn it, that it should be checked whether those who are the able-bodied or older than 60." Jankovic says: "They are able-bodied. "They are? "Yes." Djurdjic says: "So, that's the procedure. And you saw what you left in Bratunac the other day. Am I right?" And then he says: "When Toso arrives, you and him must make sure you consult some more, please." Jankovic says: "When is Toso coming? "In the early evening." Now, the evidence will show that these local staff were released when DutchBat withdrew on the 21st, but you can get a sense here from this intercept how the killing operation was hovering over everything. They knew what the procedure was supposed to be, and they weren't sure whether it was still going or not. And the man who was going to make the decision about what to do, whether these men lived or died or went to prison, was General Tolimir. Now I want to turn your attention, Your Honours, to the Zepa portion of the case. You've already seen the combat orders, the references to the fear that Zepa and Srebrenica would be linked and that they would block the Serbs access to the Drina, block their unitary state along the Drina. Once Srebrenica fell, Mladic made the decision to go on to Zepa. You'll see that General Tolimir on the 13th met with some local Muslim representatives and gave them an ultimatum. Complete evacuation of the entire population or a military solution. And we'll see a report that day from General Tolimir referring to his meeting with Hamdija Torlak, he's one of the people you'll hear about civilian representative, regarding the demilitarisation of the enclave and free movement of civilians in accordance with the Geneva Conventions from 12 August 1949." Well, you've already seen what the worth of reference is to the Geneva Conventions is, and I won't belabour that point anymore, and you will see more of that. "We have conditioned this with alternative solution - military force." Everybody leaves or we're going to attack. And then he adds that: "We guaranteed evacuation of the entire civilian population, military-aged men who surrendered their weapons, as well as safety for the civilians who decide to stay and accept the RS authority." Keep your eyes on that phrase, "stay and accept the RS authority," and see what that means. And then he says that he told the Muslims that they could register their prisoners, their fighters, and have them exchanged. But of course he says that this was a -- simply a tactical move so that they could foreclose later demands. And you'll see how genuine this offer really was. Now, remember, Your Honours, during this time even though he's in Zepa, General Tolimir has been in the communication with the Main Staff. He's being updated about the large number of Muslims who are being captured along that road that are condemned to death. This is about the time that he is going to issue his proposal to put all those prisoners inside buildings and out of sight and later this night, recall, he's going to propose separating the prisoners from other prisoners at the pig farm. So even though he is down in Zepa doing his part, he is a general, an experienced one, and he is keeping his eyes always on the big picture, both Srebrenica and Zepa at the same time. I'll just skip this map to save some time, but we'll see it soon enough. General Tolimir sends up another report about how the talks are going, how his ultimatum was received, it wasn't received well. He's keeping his command up-to-date, and he said: "If they reject the evacuation ... we are planning to start with combat activities." That's got to start by the 15th. And here he's proposing specific combat actions and axes, and he says that they should do it within 21 hours in order to avoid denouncement and reactions of the international community, again always this focus on what they can get away with if the international community is or is not looking. He's sending out more reports the next day. The Muslims aren't showing up. You'll hear that the Muslims in Zepa had begun to receive information about what happened in Potocari and reports about what was happening to the men that are unaccounted for. You'll see much evidence of how General Tolimir and the forces down there placed the UN under complete control. He refers here to check-point number 2 at Boksanica, you'll hear a lot about this check-point which he says we've already put under our control. "With these activities we plan to control the work and the reports that UNPROFOR is making to their superior command." Again, just like General Tolimir did during the Srebrenica operation, they have to neutralise UNPROFOR. His part in the Srebrenica operation was lying, delaying. Here he's working with the local command to actually physically place them under control and direct their work. You've got to get through the UN before you can get to the civilian population; that's what they're doing here. Here he's proposing that they commence combat operations as per the plan of the superior command. This is Tolimir, sense of his authority when he's in the field. Again, they're going to make it look like this check-point is functioning as if it is not blocked and surrounded by our forces. We plan to direct the work of other UN check-points through this check-point." They are in complete control. And: "We plan to keep the UN check-points at current locations in order to protect our combat formation from NATO aviation." In other words, we're going to use the peacekeepers as human shields. On the 14th of July, this is General Tolimir, again from the Rogatica Brigade command, writing personally to Miletic asking for communications equipment. In particular, he's asking for a type of radio. I think the evidence will show that this is an advanced type of radio, in particular with a KZU-63 attachment. That is a crypto-protection attachment that will encrypt what he says over the radio. He wants to be able to maintain confidentiality of what he's saying. That's natural in war, but what we know what's going on on the 14th is the executions are fully underway. He's got all manner of communications available to him and he's got encryption. And you'll see plenty of reports about the battle between the Muslim forces and the VRS between the 14th and roughly the 18th. The Muslims stormed OPs, stole the weapons, used those weapons to defend themselves. By this time they had begun receiving more detailed reports, more information about what happened in Srebrenica. And you'll hear that both sides, the Serbs and the Muslims, threatened to kill UNPROFOR peacekeepers during this battle. The Serbs threatening to kill the UNPROFOR peacekeepers if UNPROFOR called in NATO air support, again their greatest fear; on the other hand, the Muslims threatening to kill the peacekeepers if the UN didn't call in air support. And here we have this loudspeaker van being ordered by General Tolimir to help Colonel Milutinovic project their propaganda to the Muslims in Zepa that you can't stay any longer. And here we see an example of a report. This is from the Drina Corps forward command post in Krivace on the 17th. This indicates that Tolimir is with Krstic at this forward command post, talking about a conversation with Palic who is refusing to talk. Palic wants General Smith down in Zepa. We see reports on the 16th and the 17th that put General Tolimir with General Krstic, and that is critical because General Krstic himself is knee-deep in the murder operation. We'll see that General Smith gets involved at the Bosnian government's request to help deal with the Zepa situation. And you'll see on the 19th of July Mladic and Tolimir meeting with General Smith, not too far at a restaurant near Sokolac, not too far away from Zepa. At this meeting Smith confronts Mladic about what happened to the men from Srebrenica. Again, General Tolimir is present for this. Mladic insists that it was finished in a correct way. He makes some reference to the Hotel Fontana meetings. He claimed that he opened a corridor to let the troops go, accepted that some skirmishes might have taken place, but that some unfortunate small incidents had occurred. Mladic with Tolimir at his side is, as we know, as the evidence will show, was lying straight in the face of General Smith. Mladic knew all about those prisoners that he saw all along the road. He spoke to them. He addressed them as they were gathered, lied to them and told them they had nothing to worry about, those prisoners he had given the order to murder himself. Now, you'll see that on this same day everybody headed down to Zepa -- that is, I should say General Tolimir. Smith went home to Sarajevo. Tolimir goes to Zepa, and I want to show you just a short video-clip of a conversation that General Mladic had with Avdo Palic, the commander of the Zepa Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We'll not talk again. In that case you have signed a death sentence for everyone in the territory controlled by you. Do you understand me, over?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, General Mladic making it clear what the fate of the population was going to be. Now, you'll see evidence in video - we'll just skip through it now - of a meeting that General Mladic and General Tolimir had with some Muslim representatives because Palic refused to attend. You see Kosoric there with the big moustache at the end of the table, Colonel Milutinovic is sitting next to him, General Tolimir has his chin in his hand next to Mladic. After this meeting with the Muslim representatives, Mladic thinks he's got an agreement for solving the Zepa problem. He thinks that everybody's agreed to the terms he laid out - you'll hear about those terms - and he sends out a press release through the press centre. The whole logistical apparatus gets cranked up again, the buses begin arriving, the MOD agencies are notified. And you'll see that General Tolimir, as he will be throughout the rest of the Zepa operation, is personally involved in this movement of the people. On the 19th you'll see an intercept where Tolimir is selecting the route. The speakers are saying that Tolimir will select the route for the convoy. But what you'll hear is that over the next few days, even though Mladic thought he had an agreement on the 19th, there was a series of meetings in Sarajevo at the airport, where politicians on the -- and civilians on the Muslim side were meeting with the VRS representatives in Sarajevo. And the bottom line was that because the VRS could not account and refused to account for the whereabouts of the Muslim men from Srebrenica, they could not come to an agreement on how to resolve the situation in Zepa, specifically what was going to happen to the military-aged men of Zepa. The Muslims refused to let their men fall into the hands of the Serbs. They wanted to be evacuated directly by the UN by helicopters into safe territory. They had heard the stories about what had happened to the men from Srebrenica. And you'll hear that these talks collapsed on the 21st, as we see here, because the Serbs could not account for 6800 people according to the Muslims. So what we have on the 21st is General Tolimir sending a proposal from the Rogatica Brigade command personally to General Miletic, describing the military situation, saying that the Muslims are provoking action because of a conference that was going on in London. And then he suggests that the UN -- UNPROFOR and international organisation are not allowed to come into the area. "We believe that it would be more advantageous ... after we inflict losses on the enemy's military personnel." Okay. That's war talk. That's crushing your enemy. Nothing wrong with that. "The most propitious means of their destruction would be usage of chemical weapons or aerosol grenades and bombs. Using these means would accelerate the surrender of Muslims and the fall of Zepa." You will hear testimony about what those aerosol grenades and bombs were like. "We will continue with combat activities." And then, as we've seen over and over again: "We believe that we could force Muslims to surrender sooner if we would destroy groups of Muslim refugees fleeing in the direction of Stublic, Radava, and Brloska Planina." He's saying: Kill fleeing civilians. Again, not as collateral damage but as the objective. So when you see references to the Geneva Conventions, the evidence will show that that is just the falsest piety of the emptiest kind. So basically what we'll see throughout the Zepa case, Your Honours, is General Tolimir on the ground in communications with the Main Staff transmitting updates, being part of the process of decision-making. An agreement was reached with an isolated Muslim representative, Mr. Torlak. You'll see General Tolimir involved in passing that on, giving directions to the RS prisoner exchange commission about what to do. And you'll see him specifically tell the commission be careful. We have to move quickly because they keep bringing up the issue of the men from Srebrenica. A day later, this is the day that the transportations actually begin from Zepa. Tolimir is trying to make sure that a general doesn't come down. Again, he's concerned about what Morillon did in 1993. He's afraid that an UNPROFOR general will derail their plans for emptying Zepa of its Muslim population. And you'll see video, you'll hear from the witnesses that were there about the terrified population that by this time had been shelled into having no desire to stay, no hope to stay. And you'll see the video of them being taken out, again in dump trucks, lorries. He's constantly in touch with the Main Staff, getting information about what's happening. And you'll hear that one by one the "hodza," Palic, were arrested and detained after the transportations were completed. You'll see General Tolimir involved being informed of the interrogation of Colonel Palic. You'll hear testimony about how Tolimir personally separated the "hodza" from a convoy. You'll hear about him being confronted by General Gobillard about what happened to Palic and Tolimir saying, "Oh, it could be just propaganda." And then you'll hear about and you'll see in the reports General Tolimir's instruction with respect to the remaining armed and unarmed men, whoever's in the woods, "Don't register them if you capture them." Again, the Geneva Conventions are out the window. He is still in touch with Sarajevo. He's still being informed about what's going on with potential prisoner exchanges, and you'll see that the last-ditch attempt by the Serbs to make something out of a prisoner exchange is to say, "Okay, we've got a hundred high-value prisoners that we want exchanged. We'll exchange those for a similar number from the Muslim prisons for our guys." But you'll see that that can't happen right away. You'll see that General Tolimir is caught because they don't have any prisoners left. There are not enough to exchange, and you see him dealing with this issue. He can't run from it. You'll see efforts by Beara to go across the river and bring back the Muslims that have swum for their lives from Zepa. General Tolimir refers to those efforts. He's caught by it. He's got Serb families that want their sons back, but he can't get them back because he's killed all the prisoners. And General Tolimir has to be very careful about how he communicates this information because they've got the entire murder operation to conceal. And you'll see evidence about the concealment, the burial operation organised by the Main Staff through the security chain. And you'll see him writing to the exchange commission saying it's not the Main Staff's fault. It's our unit's fault for not taking enough prisoners. Simply extraordinary statement seeing as he just helped put over 7.000 POWs to death. I'm just going to skip through some of these things I've been talking about. These are intercepts that detail how Beara was trying to go across the river to get those prisoners, and you will hear one of the participants saying, "We have to get those men back because we don't have any prisoners." Even Beara's subordinate who was at the Main Staff knows they don't have any prisoners. If there's any question about the sincerity of these references to the Geneva Conventions, Your Honours, or about people being free to choose where they live, this is an aerial image of the mosque in Zepa on the 27th of July. You can see the roofs of the building of the mosque and its associated structure there on the 27th. A month later there's nothing but rubble. And if you look at the road and all these structures here, they're obliterated. You'll hear a speech from General Zivanovic on the 12th of July celebrating the fall of the Srebrenica enclave. And he says: "On my way to Srebrenica I saw the most Turkish mosque you can imagine. I was asked this morning: General, has this famous mosque been finished off? And I told them that I think that it was finished off this morning." You'll see photographs of the Srebrenica mosques in ruins. And General Zivanovic says a few moments later in this speech: "Let me tell you that with today's dusk any organised Muslim life to the left of Jadar ceased existing." And again, we can look at a 16 July combat report from Commander Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. He writes: "I consider that the Krivaja 95 operation is not complete as long as a single enemy soldier or civilian remains behind the front line." That's what it was all about, Your Honours. That's what the Krivaja 95 operation was all about. So when you see General Tolimir or another VRS officer sticking that boilerplate language about the Geneva Conventions in some documents or includes that stock paragraph that Muslims can stay in the RS if they recognise Republika Srpska authority, this is what they're talking about. Sure you can stay. Your mosques will be flattened, we'll execute your "hodza" and your other leaders, and your homes will be obliterated. That's what that meant to those officers. If I may two more minutes to conclude, Mr. President. These are some reburial operation documents. I just want to show at the height of the reburial operation in October of 1995, General Tolimir has this to say about Colonel Beara: "Highly principled ... consistent in his work, professional in the carrying out of his tasks ... "Assessed as: Excellent. "24 October 1995." This is Ratko Mladic's assessment of General Tolimir from the prior year. "The credits due to him for the Serbian people are of historic importance and immeasurable and they rank him among the most deserving individuals in our people's history." "Excellent." That's the "hodza" Tolimir personally separated found in a mass grave with Avdo Palic, here shaking the hand of General Tolimir. This is a report, you'll see it soon enough so I'll skip it, but it's a report basically memorialising the murder of a hungry unarmed Muslim in Zepa. Because that's what was going on, the extermination of whoever they could find. And this is the Batkovic prison which stayed virtually empty just a little bit north of Pilica regularly housed prisoners during the war. And just south of Pilica, just a half an hour on an asphalt road this is what the 10th Sabotage Detachment under General Tolimir's authorisation left. Your Honours, I'm just going to show you this little piece of this intercept. It's between X and Y. It doesn't really matter who. He says they're asking what to do with the wounded, the captured Turks. They're killing themselves. There's a pile of them dead. So what, the bigger the pile, the better for them. Fuck 'em. They weren't human beings." Your Honours, the utter dehumanisation that I talked about before which permeated the murder operation, the idea that your enemy is not only of a different ethnicity or religion, but is not even of the same species. You tell your men that the enemy are people who are coming to commit genocide upon you. You tell them that for four years. You tell them that the enemy is not fit to be your neighbour. That their sacred houses of worship weren't worthy, only to be rubble. Their shattered bodies are just so much refuse to be dumped in pits with rusting cars rubbish and bulldozed over. And you unleash the likes of Ljubo Beara and Vujadin Popovic to complete your plan. Make no mistake about it, Your Honours, General Tolimir was the one person next to Mladic who could have pulled Beara back from those killing fields, and instead he gave him the 10th Sabotage Detachment on the 16th of July and at Bisina on the 23rd of July. General Tolimir was in a position to save thousands. There are very few people who had the power to do that. He could have picked up the phone and called ICRC. He could have told his men under his direct professional command: Stand down. We're going to institute proceedings through the military court system. He could have proposed instead of putting people under cover on the 13th of July, hiding them away, call ICRC and get them down here. Instead of propaganda films, lives could have been saved and so could General Tolimir's honour. But that's not the plan General Tolimir chose. General Tolimir chose starvation, he chose a plan for expulsion, and he chose genocide. Thank you, Your Honours, and I thank you for the additional time.
